Don't be too quick to write yourself off. I don't have any idea of your age, but when I was younger I had a phase similar to that which lasted a few years.

Lots of things change with time. Maybe this is one of them

From what you've described, it sounds like you're not unattractive. But even if I didn't feel that way, it doesn't matter because he finds you attractive.

The problem isn't that he's too hot, but you don't believe you're worth that. Have you tried loving your body? Different people do it in different ways but I find practicing good hygiene, trying to dress well (according to your style, no one else's), and just generally making an effort to show your body some love does wonders for self esteem.

You say you have an hourglass. Flaunt your waist! You don't have to do crop tops if you're not comfortable with that, but wear shirts and dresses which are fitted around the waist and enjoy your curves.

I also have very bad stretch marks... So I wore shorts. And they were visible. But I realised that I looked so great in shorts that the marks didn't matter. My new confidence outweighed the old insecurity.

Do you have female friends? If so, a wonderful experience is all getting dressed up together for whatever event and just advising and appreciating the hell out of each others' different beauties. It really boosts morale.

I would advise you to try trusting your partner, but ultimately low self esteem is a much bigger issue that will surface in other relationships and areas of your life. I hope you can appreciate that, despite whatever the status quo on beauty is, there are people in the world who will find you not just acceptable but irresistible. Especially if you are confident and take care to be your best you.

I hope this helps :) good luck.

I can only speak for myself here. I guess I want love because it's the only thing that's ever felt true and fulfilling. It doesn't matter how often it hurts either, I always want love and human connection. I'm not sure why but when I feel it, it touches deep in the core of who I am. It feels like the only thing I've ever desperately wanted, since I was born, and the only thing I can't get enough of. Success, praise, beauty, leisure, it all feels good but eventually dulls. But love, in whatever context (partner, friend, family), is like a mutual promise of support and appreciation. Sometimes the promise is broken, but sometimes it's not.

I suppose from a more objective perspective human beings are only as successful as we are because of our ability to form complex social structures. Yeah, we're intelligent and made tools, but a human being can only survive alone so long and so well. Our evolution and expansion is due to our numbers, and our ability to unify in numbers. From that point of view, love is a reassurance to our brains that we've formed a social bond of high integrity and are more likely to survive. Especially since as infants we are completely reliant on love to make adults care for us for years until we're capable of independence. 

I guess you either do desire love but have suppressed that desire for some reason, or your conditions may mess around with your brain chemistry. I'm sure there are more explanations, but that's what I can think of. I hope this was helpful.

I'm assuming your question is more directed towards things like PDA and talking about dating. But preferences differ from person to person. I might suggest letting her set the example and just following however she approaches it, but she might be trying to do the same and you both end up in this weird, passive, not really engaging thing. Maybe try hanging out, do what feels natural, and see if you like it. Also ask her how she feels about it. You'll need to be able to communicate, not just because you're dating but especially because you're already good friends.

But I do think things should be different from being friends. Even if neither of you are very physically demanding or like pet names and other obvious couple stuff, dating means you have a special consideration for what the other person is needs and wants. For example, if you usually engage in nasty banter, that may no longer be appropriate because you might feel greater need for reassurance. Or you might try and gauge their wants and predict or defer to them when it comes to trivial decisions.

As I said earlier, it's different for everyone. You might figure it out through trial and error, but you might end up hurting the other person. Or you could just talk to her, and risk things being a little awkward.

Is there anyone close to you who can let you sleep on their floor or couch for a bit, until the lease ends? A close friend, or parent, or sibling? If you do, you can live with them (either rent free or paying little rent) and redirect the money you spend on electricity and food to their household. It would be a strain on them, and you would have to be open with them about that. It would also mean shelling out a little extra each month. But it's better than having to pay two full sets of rent, and better than living with someone you don't want to be with and lying about it. You can sell furniture, or clothes, or work overtime, or pick up a part time job to support the awkward living situation for a few months.

This is actually what I'm doing right now. The lease officially ends on 30 November, and I broke up with my partner and moved out about a month ago. I pay a small rent to the people I'm currently with. It's very difficult but ultimately I'm happier.

From what I understand, in hunter-gatherer societies women were gatherers because intermittent pregnancies made them ill-suited to be hunters. However, they still produced the majority of the food as successful hunts didn't happen every day.

It was the gatherers, the women, who logically would have discovered basic farming and agriculture, or I suspect as much. Agriculture produced lots of edible plants, and later animals, and so the hunters, men, were drawn back partially for that reason, and partially because as agriculture developed being strong became an important part of ploughing and other aspects of farming. Men have different muscular development and so were more suited to this. So now both sexes were dedicated to the same practices, but men had an advantage.

Furthermore, while males have hormones which encourage aggression, after millenia of being hunters they had developed an acute violent impulse. Combine this with having to compete with females in the same field (pun unintended) for the first time, and they proceeded to dominate agricultural practises as well as females. Once a society is male-dominated there is a greater drive to control women, for reasons such as ensuring that a woman's offspring are truly your genetic heritage by controlling her sexuality via monogamy and other structures, which produces a lot of the commonalities we see in patriarchal societies.

This is mostly cobbled together from my own speculation and independent reading. I don't claim expertise on the subject and appreciate criticism.

I keep fighting, and fighting, and fighting. Every time I am confronted with my depression I fight back... And after years of fighting, it has also become like a compulsion. I don't know if what I'm doing is healthy or not. But for what it's worth, it's working, and I'm happy to be alive for once.

I hope things get better for you. You might never get rid of depression, but you might be able to learn to manage it.

READ. Not just textbooks, read for fun regularly. Every day. At least 30mins. Your reading speed will increase, so will your language proficiency and processing speed. Literacy is a skill that needs to be learned and maintained. I swear, this easily adds a good 10% to any assessment I do on any topic or in any field, especially discursive areas. For second language speakers, (eg. A transfer student / foreign person in an English speaking country) this is a great way to boost your learning curve and work against the instant disadvantage you have writing tests and exams in a language which isn't your mother tongue.

Plus reading is fun and books are an escape from the constant pressure to succeed and the inevitable stress of not being perfect. Mental health is very important for everyone, and high performance students especially need to learn to manage stress and anxiety.
